clue.text: Criticise Kane, possibly, for showboating spot kick

parts.note: to pan is to criticise harshly

indicators.note: possibly signals that the name Kane may be rearranged into another order

parts.note: Harry Kane, the England striker, whose letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: A pundit is invited to criticise England striker Harry Kane for a flashy penalty attempt.
explanation.walkthrough: PAN is followed by ENKA, the rearrangement of KANE signalled by 'possibly'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Panenka is a penalty chipped softly down the middle, named after the Czech player Antonin Panenka; it is the classic cheeky penalty.

clue.text: Particular types of briefs probed by leading journo

indicators.note: probed by means the briefs word has the journo's letters pushed inside it

parts.note: briefs are underpants, pants
the editor, ED, is the leading journalist on a paper

explanation.surface: Fussy people's underwear is investigated by a top reporter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Particular' looks like 'specific', but it means fussy.
explanation.definitionFit: Pedants are fussy people who insist on minor details and exact rules.

clue.text: No obstruction set up for traveller

indicators.note: set up in a down clue means the word for obstruction reads upwards, backwards

parts.note: a dam is a barrier obstructing a river

explanation.surface: A traveller finds the road clear, with no barrier put in place.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'set up' turns DAM bottom to top, giving MAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A nomad is a wanderer with no fixed home who moves from place to place.

clue.text: Older relative is silly, having no boundaries

indicators.note: having no boundaries means the first and last letters of the word for silly are cut off

parts.note: inane means silly or senseless

explanation.surface: An elderly family member is being foolish and acting without limits.
explanation.definitionFit: Nan is an informal word for grandmother, a relative from an older generation.

clue.text: Podcaster is keen to host a star

indicators.note: to host means the words podcaster is keen contain the answer within them

explanation.surface: An online broadcaster is eager to have a celebrity guest on the show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a star' looks like the celebrity guest, but it is the printed symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: An asterisk is the small star-shaped typographical symbol used to mark footnotes.

clue.text: We are nearly about to reject an online meeting

indicators.note: about means the shortened we are goes around the next piece
nearly means the last letter of we are is dropped, leaving it incomplete

parts.note: taken as the letters WEARE
to bin something is to reject or throw it away

explanation.surface: Someone announces that a group has nearly decided to turn down an invitation to a video call.
explanation.walkthrough: WEAR (We are minus its final E) wraps around BIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A webinar is a seminar held over the internet, so it is a virtual meeting or presentation.

clue.text: You and I had essentially left with almost all of the cash

parts.note: you and I together are we

indicators.note: essentially means the central letter, the essence, of had
almost all of means the word the loses its final letter

parts.note: taken without its last letter, giving TH

explanation.surface: We basically walked off with nearly all the money.
explanation.definitionFit: Wealth is an abundance of money or possessions, plenty of riches.

clue.text: Airbuses flying around one elevated capital city

indicators.note: around means the shuffled letters go around the reversed one
flying suggests the letters of airbuses moving freely into a new arrangement

parts.note: anagram fodder

indicators.note: elevated in a down clue means the word one is raised, read bottom to top

explanation.surface: Passenger jets circle above a capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged AIRBUSES surround ENO, which is 'one' read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Buenos Aires is the capital of Argentina, the country's largest city.

clue.text: Losing at running is followed by a feeling of sadness

indicators.note: is followed by places the letter A after the rearranged letters
running suggests losing at being set in motion into a fresh order

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Losing at a race brings on a melancholy feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: Nostalgia is a wistful longing for the past, a bittersweet sadness for times gone by.

clue.text: Mark wears torn clothing

indicators.note: wears means the word for mark is held within the word for torn, like a garment worn

parts.note: rent is an old past participle of rend, meaning torn
a mark is a target, an aim

explanation.surface: A man named Mark is wearing ripped clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a man's name, but it means a target.
explanation.definitionFit: Raiment is an archaic or literary word for garments and dress.

clue.text: Nasty person, say, steals the last part of our show

parts.note: a demon is a wicked or nasty person

indicators.note: steals means the word for say takes another letter into itself

parts.note: to state is to say

indicators.note: the last part of means only the final letter of our is used

parts.note: its last letter is R

explanation.surface: A villainous person makes off with the finale of a theatre company's production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'show' looks like a noun after 'our', but it is a verb meaning to prove or exhibit; 'say' is the verb state, not 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: To demonstrate is to show how something works or to prove it by example.

clue.text: After only a half of Skol, I go downhill

indicators.note: After places the letter I following the half of Skol in the answer
a half of means only the first two of Skol's four letters are kept

parts.note: a lager brand, here cut to its front half

explanation.surface: Someone who has drunk just half a lager says they are now off down the slopes.
explanation.walkthrough: Skol is a lager brand and also a drinking toast; 'a half' plays on ordering half a pint. 'go downhill' looks like decline, but here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: To ski is to travel down snowy slopes on long runners, quite literally descending a hill.

clue.text: New bus-driver occasionally not decent?

indicators.note: occasionally means only every other letter of bus-driver is taken

parts.note: its alternate letters are U, D, I, E

explanation.surface: A query whether a new bus driver is improperly dressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not decent' plays on the phrase for being undressed when someone knocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Nudie is an informal adjective for naked or featuring nudity, and someone unclothed is said to be not decent.

clue.text: Church leader initially favouring inferior sort of wine

parts.note: an elder is a senior lay official in some churches

indicators.note: initially means only the first letter of favouring

parts.note: lower means of lesser rank, inferior

explanation.surface: A church official tends to prefer a cheap kind of wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Elderflower wine is a homemade country wine brewed from the blossoms of the elder tree.

clue.text: Judge taking possession of a place in Scotland with large grounds

indicators.note: taking possession of means the word for judge holds the following pieces inside it

parts.note: to rate something is to judge or assess it
Iona is a small island in the Inner Hebrides of Scotland
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A judge acquires a Scottish estate with extensive grounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grounds' looks like land attached to the estate, but it means reasons.
explanation.definitionFit: A rationale is the reasoning behind a decision, which is what grounds for an action are.

clue.text: Chips perhaps made by two guys? Pretty much!

parts.note: Sid and Ed are two short male names
ish is a colloquial word meaning more or less, pretty much

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether fries were cooked by two men, and gets the vague answer 'more or less'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty much!' reads as a reply, but it is the informal word ISH, used on its own to mean 'sort of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chips (fries) are a typical accompaniment served alongside a main course, an example of this kind of dish.

clue.text: Venture to secure unknown amount of money for social enterprise

indicators.note: to secure means the word for venture grips the following letters inside it

parts.note: to dare is to venture
Y is an algebraic unknown
a cent is a small sum of money

explanation.surface: A business venture seeks funding for a community project.
explanation.definitionFit: A day centre is a facility offering daytime care and activities for elderly or vulnerable people, a social service.

clue.text: Was an instructor wrong when speaking?

indicators.note: when speaking means the word for a legal wrong is said aloud, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: A question whether a teacher got it wrong while giving a talk.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent the legal term and the answer sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Taught is the past tense of teach, and to teach is what an instructor does.

clue.text: At any point, fabled monster's home is said to disappear

indicators.note: is said means the two words together are spoken aloud to give a word of the same sound

parts.words: At any point, fabled monster's home
parts.note: ever means at any point, and Ness, the Scottish loch, is home of the legendary Loch Ness Monster; together they are heard as one word

explanation.surface: A legendary beast's lair is said to vanish at any moment.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken in a non-rhotic accent, EVER plus NESS sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To evanesce is to fade away or vanish like vapour, a literary verb.

clue.text: Rules primarily protected by county's elected officials

indicators.note: protected by means the first letter of rules is held inside the county's name

parts.note: Mayo is a county in the west of Ireland; with its possessive S

indicators.note: primarily means only the first letter of rules is used

explanation.surface: Regulations are mainly safeguarded by the elected people of a county.
explanation.walkthrough: Mayo is an Irish county; the apostrophe S is kept as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayors are civic heads of towns or cities, chosen by voters or councillors.

clue.text: Parent and child in charge of a secret group

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother, a parent
a son is a child

explanation.surface: A mother and her son run a clandestine society.
explanation.definitionFit: Masonic is an adjective relating to Freemasons, a fraternal society known for its secret rites.

clue.text: Dull players going after a number of balls

indicators.note: going after places the players' word after the cricket term

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled by one bowler
the cast is the set of actors in a production

explanation.surface: Boring actors chasing after a bunch of balls.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an OVER is six consecutive deliveries from one bowler.
explanation.definitionFit: Overcast describes a grey, cloudy sky, which is dull weather.

clue.text: Touching, explosive letters full of endless outrage

indicators.note: full of means the explosive letters contain the following piece

parts.note: TNT is the abbreviation for the explosive trinitrotoluene

indicators.note: endless means the last letter of the word for outrage is dropped

parts.note: anger is outrage

explanation.surface: Emotive letters bursting with constant fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Touching' looks like 'moving', but in geometry a tangent touches a curve.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangent line meets a curve at one point, so as an adjective it means touching, in contact.

clue.text: Darling socialist providing support for a party

indicators.note: providing support for in a down clue puts the socialist word beneath, below a party

parts.note: a do is a party
red is a common term for a socialist or communist

explanation.surface: A beloved left-winger backs a political party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'party' looks political, but DO is a social gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: Adored means dearly loved, as a darling is.

clue.text: Group of teen lads swimming round end of jetty

indicators.note: round means the shuffled letters go around the final letter of jetty
swimming suggests the letters of teen lads moving about freely into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder

indicators.note: end of means only the last letter of jetty, Y

explanation.surface: Teenage boys swim around the far tip of a pier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' puts the rearranged TEEN LADS around Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Steely Dan is an American rock band of the 1970s, so it is a musical group.

clue.text: Protest is about money

indicators.note: about means the word is is turned around back to front

parts.note: tin is old British slang for money

explanation.surface: A statement that a demonstration is really all about cash.
explanation.walkthrough: TIN is dated British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: A sit-in is a form of protest where demonstrators occupy a place and refuse to leave.

clue.text: Feature of señorita's hat incorporating diamonds

indicators.note: incorporating means the word for hat takes in the diamonds letter

parts.note: tile is old British slang for a hat
D is the card-suit abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: A Spanish woman's hat is decorated with diamonds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feature of señorita's' looks like a hat or face, but it is the mark over the N.
explanation.definitionFit: The tilde is the wavy accent over the n in the Spanish word señorita.

clue.text: Invest from time to time and make a score?

indicators.note: from time to time means only every other letter of invest is used

parts.note: its even-placed letters are taken, skipping every other one

explanation.surface: Asking whether occasional investing will earn twenty pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'score' looks like twenty, but it is a goal: to net is to put the ball in the net.
explanation.definitionFit: In football, to net is to put the ball in the goal, which scores.

clue.text: A field scattered with worms? I can't believe it!

indicators.note: scattered signals the letters of a field and worms strewn about in a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A gardener's astonishment at a field strewn with worms.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram covers A FIELD and WORMS together; 'with' joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom expresses being too astonished or shocked to speak, an exclamation of disbelief.

clue.text: Awesome slice of chocolate cake served up

indicators.note: served up in a down clue means the slice is read upwards, backwards
slice of means a piece is taken from inside chocolate cake

explanation.surface: A wonderful piece of chocolate gateau is brought to the table.
explanation.walkthrough: The slice ECA spans the end of 'chocolate' and the start of 'cake'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ace is informal slang for excellent or brilliant.

clue.text: Cocaine dealer somehow not convicted?

parts.note: C is slang shorthand for cocaine

indicators.note: somehow implies the letters of dealer arranged in some other way

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A question whether a drug dealer somehow escaped conviction.
explanation.definitionFit: A defendant cleared by a court is found not guilty, acquitted of the charge.

clue.text: Difficult achievement always takes energy and, ultimately, excess time

parts.note: ever means always, as in for ever
E is the physics symbol for energy

indicators.note: ultimately means only the last letter of excess is taken

explanation.surface: A hard-won feat always demands effort and, in the end, too much time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes' joins EVER to the letters that follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: Climbing the world's highest mountain is the proverbial supreme challenge, so any formidable goal is called an Everest.
